book_intro:
Yazar, Tarih ve Alıcılar

Luka bir doktordu (Kol. 4:14) ve elçi Pavlus'un yol arkadaşıydı. Bu İncil'i ve onun devamı olan Elçilerin İşleri kitabını yazmıştır. Luka-Elçilerin İşleri'nin olası en erken tarihi, Luka'nın Elçilerin İşleri 28'de kaydettiği olaylardan hemen sonradır ki, bu da yaklaşık M.S. 62 yılıdır. Hem Luka hem de Elçilerin İşleri hakkında başka bir şey bilinmeyen "Teofilos "a (Luka 1:3; Elçilerin İşleri 1:1) hitaben yazılmıştır. Luka'nın geniş dinleyici kitlesi öncelikle Teofilus gibi İsa hakkında "öğretilmiş" (Luka 1:4) olan Yahudi olmayan Hıristiyanlardan oluşuyordu.

Tema

Müjde hem Yahudiler hem de Yahudi olmayanlar içindir, çünkü İsa, Eski Antlaşma'da peygamberlik edildiği ve Tanrı'nın İsa'nın yaşamı, ölümü ve dirilişindeki kurtarıcı faaliyetinde görüldüğü gibi Tanrı'nın vaat ettiği kişidir. Luka'nın okuyucularının aldığı Hıristiyan gelenekleri doğrudur; Tanrı'nın Oğlu İsa Mesih'e iman ederek, O'nu izleyen herkese vereceği vaat edilen Kutsal Ruh'u alacaklardır.

Amaç

Luka'nın yazarken muhtemelen birkaç amacı vardı: (1) okuyucularını kendilerine öğretilenlerin doğruluğu konusunda temin etmek; (2) İsrail'in İsa'yı reddetmesinin ve Yahudi olmayanların Tanrı'nın krallığına girmesinin Tanrı'nın planının bir parçası olduğunu anlamalarına yardımcı olmak; (3) İsa'nın bedensel dönüşünün hemen olacağını değil, dirilişi ile dönüşü arasında bir dönem olacağını öğrettiğini açıklığa kavuşturmak; ve (4) Roma gibi herhangi bir dünyevi güçten korkmamaları gerektiğini vurgulamak.

Anahtar Temalar

Tanrı'nın tarih üzerindeki egemen yönetimi (13:33; 22:22; 42).

Tanrı'nın Egemenliği'nin gelişi ve gerçek varlığı (henüz tamamlanmamış olsa da) (11:2; 17:20-21; 21:34-36).

İsa ve takipçileri için Kutsal Ruh'un gelişi ve varlığı (1:15-17; 35; 2:25-27; 3:16; 22; 4:1; 18; 24:49).

İlklerin sonuncu ve sonuncuların ilk olduğu, gururluların alçaltıldığı ve alçakgönüllülerin yüceltildiği dünyada meydana gelen büyük değişim (1:48; 6:20-26; 13:30; 14:11).

İnanlılar duayla dolu bir yaşam sürmeli ve sahip oldukları mallarla iyi bir kâhyalık yapmalıdırlar (6:12; 9:28-29; 11:1-4; 12:33-34; 18:1; 22:40).

Zenginlik tehlikesi (6:20-26; 8:14; 12:13-21; 16:10-13; 19-31).

Anahatlar

Önsöz (1:1-4)

Bebeklik Anlatısı (1:5-2:52)

İsa'nın Hizmeti İçin Hazırlık (3:1-4:15)

İsa'nın Celile'deki Hizmeti (4:16-9:50)

Yeruşalim'e Yolculuk (9:51-19:27)

İsa'nın Yeruşalim'deki Hizmeti (19:28-21:38)

İsa'nın Acı Çekmesi ve Ölümü (22:1-23:56)

İsa'nın Dirilişi (24:1-53)

Luka'nın Ortamı

Luka kitabındaki olayların neredeyse tamamı, kabaca kuzeyde Caesarea Philippi'den güneyde Beersheba'ya kadar uzanan bir bölge olan Filistin çevresinde geçer. Bu süre zarfında bölge Roma İmparatorluğu tarafından yönetilmekteydi. Başlangıç bölümleri İsa'nın, Hirodes'in Romalılar tarafından kral olarak atandığı Yahudiye'de doğumunu çevreleyen olayları anlatır. Kapanış bölümleri İsa'nın ölümü, dirilişi ve Pontius Pilatus ile Antipas ve Filipus tetrarklarının yönetimi sırasında göğe yükselişiyle sona erer.

passages.title: The Journey to Jerusalem.
passages.text: During his ministry of teaching, healing, and making disciples, Jesus “set his face” (9:51) for his final journey to Jerusalem.

notes.text: seventy-two. Many very old and reliable Greek manuscripts have “seventy-two” here and in v. 17, while many other old and reliable manuscripts have “seventy.” In any case, the number probably represents all the nations in the world (compare Genesis 10). Sending them out two by two fulfills the OT requirement for two witnesses (Deut. 19:15).

I am sending you. Although only the Twelve are named “apostles” (6:13; 9:10; 22:14; Acts 1:26), others are also “sent ones.” as lambs in the midst of wolves. Jesus warns them of the dangers they face.

No sandals probably means not to take an extra pair, since Jesus is telling them what they should not carry. They are to greet no one. Such greetings were lengthy and time-consuming (see 2 Kings 4:29).
Peace. See note on John 14:27.
son of peace. One who has found the peace that comes with salvation. it will return to you. If faith is not present, the blessing will be useless.
for the laborer deserves his wages. Paul alludes to this saying in 1 Cor. 9:14 and quotes it as “Scripture” in 1 Tim. 5:18.

Heal the sick assumes the same power and authority as in 9:1 (compare 10:19). The kingdom of God has come refers to his reign in people’s hearts, not to geographical territory. See 9:2; 11:20; 16:16; 17:21. The “kingdom of God” in this present age is precisely the rule and reign of God in people’s hearts and lives.
go into its streets. The symbolic act of judgment against a town will be visible and public (compare 9:5).
the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. A sign of judgment on those rejecting the gospel (compare Acts 13:51).
more bearable on that day. Greater understanding of God’s revelation means greater responsibility.

Tyre and Sidon. On these cities, see notes on Matt. 11:20–24; Mark 7:24. sitting in sackcloth and ashes. An expression of mourning and repentance. “Sackcloth” is rough cloth made from goat’s hair; “ashes” were either placed on the head (2 Sam. 13:19) or sat upon (Job 2:8; Jonah 3:6).

Capernaum will receive the severest judgment because they witnessed Jesus’ ministry and miracles to such a great extent (4:23; 7:1–10) yet rejected him. brought down to Hades. The place of the unrighteous dead (16:22–26).
The one who hears you hears me emphasizes the unity of Jesus and his disciples.

I saw Satan fall. It is not clear whether Jesus is speaking of a vision by which he saw something in the spiritual realm or if this is simply a declaration of what has been happening. In either case, Satan’s authority and power over people has been broken.
Serpents and scorpions are physical dangers that the disciples will face in their preaching, and also symbols of demonic opposition. nothing shall hurt you. See 21:18; Acts 28:3–5.
your names are written in heaven. Compare Phil. 4:3; Rev. 3:5; 20:15.

rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. See 3:22; 4:1; 18. Father. See note on Matt. 6:9. Lord of heaven and earth. Compare Acts 17:24. Jesus’ rejoicing is due primarily to God’s having revealed (Luke 10:22) the presence of the kingdom and Satan’s fall (vv. 17–18) to little children, that is, to the disciples, who have childlike faith (v. 23). wise and understanding. Wise in the world’s eyes but unwilling to accept the gospel. Compare 1 Cor. 1:19.
All things . . . handed over to me. See note on Matt. 11:27. anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Compare John 14:6; Acts 4:12.
The parable of the good Samaritan is an example of how the “wise and understanding” (v. 21) do not understand even the simplest commands of Scripture (compare v. 27 with Lev. 19:18).
what shall I do? Compare 18:18; Acts 16:30. eternal life. Compare Luke 18:18, 30; see note on John 3:16.
What is written in the Law? For Jesus, the OT is the standard of faith and practice (compare 18:19–20).

Matthew, Mark, and Luke all include the words heart (emotions, will, and deepest convictions), soul (the immaterial part of a person’s being), and mind (reason; this term is lacking in Deut. 6:5). Matthew (22:37) alone lacks the term strength.
do this, and you will live. Jesus is about to show the lawyer that he falls far short of following these commands (see note on Mark 10:19).
who is my neighbor? A deceitful question, because the lawyer was trying to eliminate responsibility for others by making some people “non-neighbors” (see note on v. 36).

Jericho. See note on Matt. 20:29. The Jericho road, still visible today, included long stretches of rocky terrain that made it convenient for robbers. The road descended (down) about 3,200 feet (975 m) in the 18 miles (29 km) from Jerusalem to Jericho.
passed by on the other side. A good picture of the priest’s unwillingness to love his neighbor.
Levite. A member of the tribe of Levi. The Levites assisted the priests.

It would have been unthinkable for a Samaritan to help a Jew (see John 4:9; 8:48; see note on John 4:4). Loving one’s neighbor involves showing care and compassion even to those with whom one would not normally have any relationship, but who are now in need (compare Luke 6:27, 35).
two denarii. The equivalent of two days’ wages.
Which of these . . . proved to be a neighbor? Jesus’ question corrects the lawyer’s deceitful question (v. 29). The question is not “who is my neighbor?” but “how can I be a neighbor?”

village. Bethany (see John 12:1; see note on John 11:1). who sat at the Lord’s feet. A disciple’s proper place (compare Luke 8:35; Acts 22:3); unlike some in his culture, Jesus encouraged women to study the Scriptures. you are anxious . . . about many things. See Luke 8:14; 12:11; 22–30; 21:34. Mary has chosen the good portion echoes OT passages where close fellowship with the Lord is one’s “portion” in life (see Ps. 16:5; 73:26; 142:5). Mary has chosen this, and it will not be taken away from her—neither now (to help Martha in the kitchen) nor for all eternity.
